newsitem.title: USA: Three dead in Alabama plane crash.
newsitem.headline: Three dead in Alabama plane crash.

text.p: A private twin-engine plane crashed into a home in an inner-city neighbourhood shortly after takeoff on Monday, killing all three people on board, emergency officials said.
The county coroner's office was awaiting dental records to help identify the three victims.

The pilot of the Piper PA-34, struggling to keep the plane aloft with one of its engines out, put in an emergency call to air traffic controllers five minutes before the aircraft plunged into an area of the city known as the West End.
Airport officials said the disabled plane veered past a downtown office building while trying to turn around and head back to Birmingham International Airport.
"He was having difficulty gaining altitude," Doug Whitson, general manager of the airport control tower, said.

As the plane descended into the West End residential area, it clipped a tree and then the chimney of a house before slamming into another home and bursting into flames. As many as nine people, including two children, were inside the wood bungalow when the plane came down at 7:20 a.m. CST. All managed to escape the structure, which was gutted by the fire.
The home was next door to the Cleveland Avenue Christian Academy, a day-care centre which was empty at the time.

"The faster we ran, the closer the fire got to us, like it was running after us," said Tomeka Phillips, who was inside the house with her family. "I thank the Lord every time I blink my eyelashes. I thank the Lord we're alright."
The Federal Aviation Administration said the plane had taken off for Pensacola, Fla., when it crashed within five miles of the Birmingham airport.

"The airplane was taking off from Birmingham and declared an emergency due to an engine out and crashed into a residential area. There were three fatalities and two houses damaged," said George Prellezo, regional director of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) in Miami.
An NTSB investigator was dispatched to the site in hopes of determining the cause of the crash.
"We think the plane might have been trying to land in this area," Birmingham police chief Johnnie Johnson said. "We don't know the cause."
